extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literature students, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic guide to the principal aspects a novelist must consider — story, voice, space, and people — and how common human experiences (birth, food, sleep, love, death) are typically handled in fiction. Uses examples (Tolstoy, Stein, Defoe, Trollope) to illustrate good and bad practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of space
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's possession of a 'sense of space' — an expansive, accumulated presentation of place that gives grandeur and sonority beyond episodes and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space can produce an exhilarating, music-like effect (example: War and Peace) when the sum-total of setting (bridges, frozen rivers, forests, roads, gardens, fields) accumulates; few novelists achieve this, and it ranks high among a novelist's equipment. Cultivate a pervasive sense of space rather than merely a feeling for discrete places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as sequence/time
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel 'tells a story' — a simple sequence ('and then... and then') in time is the fundamental contribution of the story-aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore the time-sequence: it is primitive and essential to narrative intelligibility. While other aspects (character, value) press against story, abolishing sequence undermines meaning. Use chronology deliberately; sequence helps readers follow events and derive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on abolishing time and order (experimentation caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Radical attempts to abolish chronological sequence and even word/sentence order (example: Gertrude Stein) risk making fiction unintelligible and therefore valueless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental dismantling of time can be a noble experiment but tends to 'fail' because removing sequence removes the vehicle for expressing anything; if you attempt such experiments, be aware you may also need to reinvent other structures to replace what chronology supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as oral voice (the tale-read aloud quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is the repository of a voice that appeals to the ear and asks to be read aloud; it adds something by connecting the narrative to a 'tribal narrator' voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the story's oral quality: some sentences or openings lose power if not read aloud. The voice converts readers into listeners and provides an effect distinct from the author's personality or prose melody. Use rhythm and phrasing that sustain this oral dimension where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should reveal hidden life (novelist's privilege)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the historian who infers character from actions, the novelist's function is to reveal the 'hidden life' — inner thoughts, dreams, passions — producing characters who are not the historical person but fuller fictional beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the novelist's licence to expose inner life and motivations; this is how characters become more definite than historical figures or real friends. Balance believable exterior actions with interior revelations to create convincing fictional people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as creations conditioned by the novelist
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are 'word-masses' created from the novelist's guesses about others and himself; their nature is further modified by other aspects of the work (plot, form, authorial temperament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember characters carry traces of the novelist's temperament and are shaped by wider formal choices. When designing characters, account for how plot, voice, and the author's perspective will modify them; avoid thinking of characters as independent, purely 'real' entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of animals as actors (current limits and future potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although animals have been used in fiction, they have had limited success and are often rendered as symbolic, anthropomorphic ('little men disguised'), or decorative; future scientific knowledge may enable more authentic animal characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you introduce non-human actors, be mindful of the common pitfalls (symbolism, thin anthropomorphism). Consider how advances in knowledge might permit richer depictions, but do not default to caricatured or merely symbolic animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of birth in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Birth in novels is seldom explored psychologically; babies often appear 'like parcels' (delivered 'off') and are then laid aside until useful to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Birth is typically perfunctory in fiction; if you attempt to depict birth or the infant's psychology, be aware it is unusual and difficult. Consider whether exploring birth can yield new literary material, but expect challenges in reconstructing infant consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of death in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Death is handled more fully and observationally in novels; it conveniently ends books and allows the novelist, who understands characters by then, to be both appropriate and imaginative (example: Mrs. Proudie's death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use death as a structural and emotional terminus: because the novelist often knows the character well by the end, death scenes can be both faithful and imaginative. Avoid inserting dubious 'seance' details about an afterlife; imaginative fidelity matters more than pseudo-information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of food in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Food in fiction is mainly social: it draws characters together, but is seldom shown physiologically or sensuously; characters rarely enjoy or digest food unless the author specifically attends to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to use meals for realism or sensuous detail, do so deliberately: food can function aesthetically (taste, sensuousness) and socially. Don't let meals be merely stage-setting; exploit their capacity to reveal relations and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sleep and dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: Sleep is usually perfunctory in novels; dreams appear as logical symbols or mosaics serving a purpose rather than a sustained attempt to reconstruct dreaming as a significant part of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that fiction tends to privilege waking life; if you choose to depict sleep/dream life, be conscious that it is uncommon and requires imaginative work to avoid clichés. Use dreams with clear purpose relative to awake-life representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of love (including sex) in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Love — especially sexual love — is given disproportionate prominence in novels, often making them monotonous; it is unduly prominent because characters are created sensitive to it and because love conveniently supplies permanence for endings (marriage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of over-reliance on love as the central engine of plot. Examine whether the prominence of love reflects the novelist's own composing state or serves merely to provide tidy endings. Aim for complexity and realism in emotional life rather than constant heightened sensitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homo Fictus vs Homo Sapiens (fictional human traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional people (Homo Fictus) differ from real people: they are often 'born off', can die on-, require little food or sleep, are tireless about human relationships, and are more fully knowable because creator and narrator are one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously manage the liberties you take with fictional humans: their concentrated intelligibility is a tool, but avoid making them implausibly exempt from ordinary needs unless the work demands that stylization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character concreteness and physicality (Moll Flanders example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-drawn characters have physical presence and everyday gestures ('height and weight, as breathing and eating') and can move readers by vivid, modest details and humour rather than by heavy-handed psychological analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concreteness—use physical details, plausible behaviour, and economical humour to make characters convincing. The example of Moll Flanders shows an engaging character shaped by anecdote, action, and the author's experience rather than elaborate modern psychologizing.
